final_answer:
Short answer: Probably not as a categorical matter, but the facts as stated make a First Amendment (and Fourth Amendment) violation plausible and, on the thin record given, likely if the dispersal order and arrests rested only on generalized concern about traffic and 'potential escalation.' The outcome turns on facts not in the hypothetical.

1. Governing framework. A peaceful protest in a public forum such as a plaza and sidewalk is core protected speech and assembly. Police may not disperse or punish peaceful demonstrators merely because of anticipated disorder or listener hostility. Edwards v. South Carolina, 372 U.S. 229 (1963) (reversing breach-of-peace convictions of peaceful protesters where there was no violence or threat of violence); Cox v. Louisiana, 379 U.S. 536 (1965) (a dispersal order based on an erroneous conclusion that peaceful speech was a breach of the peace could not support conviction; police could have controlled hostile onlookers). Collins v. Jordan, 110 F.3d 1363 (9th Cir. 1996) (persuasive): First Amendment activity may not be banned simply because earlier similar activity involved violence. However, government may impose content-neutral time, place and manner restrictions and may act when speech is likely to cause imminent lawless action or actual disorder; the line is imminent threat, not speculation. (Brandenburg v. Ohio, Ward v. Rock Against Racism, and Feiner v. New York are standard companion authorities but I did not verify them in this run.)

2. Application. Facts favoring the protesters: the protest was generally peaceful; signs and chanting are classic expression; the only 'disorder' was occasional stepping into the street and a couple of verbal arguments with passers-by; the stated reasons were traffic and potential escalation, which are predictive rather than evidence of present unlawful conduct; the protest ran a couple of hours without a dispersal order. Under Edwards and Cox, verbal arguments and mere hostile or uncomfortable reactions do not make an assembly unlawful, and a generalized fear of escalation is the sort of rationale those cases reject. Facts favoring the city: repeated entry into the roadway can be real obstruction of traffic, which the city may regulate in a content-neutral way (Illinois/Chicago disorderly-conduct and obstruction provisions); Illinois law criminalizes a participant in a mob action who does not withdraw when commanded by a peace officer (720 ILCS 5/25-1, Class A misdemeanor), but mob action requires force or violence, or an assembly to commit a crime or do violence, none of which is described; Chicago Municipal Code 8-4-010 (as I recall it, not verified in this run) penalizes failure to obey a lawful dispersal order where three or more persons are committing acts of disorderly conduct likely to cause substantial harm or serious inconvenience, annoyance or alarm. Disorderly conduct under 720 ILCS 5/26-1 requires knowingly acting in such an unreasonable manner as to alarm or disturb another and provoke a breach of the peace; occasional street entry and argument are weak support. A dispersal order is lawful only if the predicate unlawful conduct is actually present; an order resting on protected activity is not a lawful order, and arrests for disobeying it lack probable cause or are retaliatory.

3. Seventh Circuit authority. Vodak v. City of Chicago, 639 F.3d 738 (7th Cir. 2011) (Posner, J.), arising from the 2003 Iraq-war march and ~900 mass arrests, recognized that dispersal orders and mass arrests of a crowd that included peaceful protesters raise serious probable-cause questions and that police must have probable cause as to the people arrested, while also treating qualified immunity and the possibility that part of a crowd was committing offenses as important. Thayer v. Chiczewski, 705 F.3d 237 (7th Cir. 2012), involved Chicago's dispersal-order ordinance and First Amendment retaliation claims by arrested protesters and illustrates that arrests without a prior dispersal order, or without actual disorderly conduct, are vulnerable. I could not retrieve the full text of either opinion (blocked sources), so the precise holdings stated here are from search summaries and my recollection and should be verified before reliance.

4. Remedies and procedure. A challenge would typically be a 42 U.S.C. 1983 suit (First and Fourth Amendment, plus possible Monell claim against the City) or a defense to prosecution. Key obstacles: (a) probable cause for any offense, even a different one, defeats a Fourth Amendment false-arrest claim (Devenpeck v. Alford; District of Columbia v. Wesby; not verified here) and, under Nieves v. Bartlett, generally defeats retaliatory-arrest claims absent narrow exceptions; (b) qualified immunity, since courts often find no clearly established law on particular crowd-control facts, as in Vodak; (c) the proper analysis of the order is as a time/place/manner restriction, which is valid only if content-neutral, narrowly tailored to a significant interest, and leaving open alternative channels. Narrow tailoring is hard to satisfy for a blanket dispersal of a whole peaceful assembly when police could have addressed the street-blocking subset or provided a sidewalk-only instruction. Also relevant: the order must be clear, audible, and give a reasonable opportunity to comply (loudspeaker, a stated route and time), and Chicago's ordinance is limited to a lawful order; vagueness issues (Grayned; Chicago v. Morales) are possible but unverified here.

Conclusion: The mere fact that the protest was lawful in origin does not immunize persistent street obstruction, and the city can validly regulate traffic. But if the record shows only occasional stepping off the curb, a couple of arguments, and speculative escalation concerns, the unlawful-assembly declaration was unsupported and the dispersal and arrests likely violated the First Amendment (and lacked probable cause), though individual officers may well obtain qualified immunity and the City's liability depends on policy or practice. Verify current Chicago Municipal Code and any post-2025 case law; none specific to July 12, 2025 was researched.
